context: Al-Qiyamah is Makkan and answers one objection rather than unbelief in general. The people of Makkah were not confused about whether there is a God. What they refused was that a body gone to bone and then to dust could be reassembled. The surah quotes them: does man think that We will not assemble his bones. Verse six adds the taunt, a demand for the date.

Because the objection is physical, so is the reply. Nothing argues from scripture or from justice. The evidence is the fingertips of a hand and the drop of fluid a person began as. Four verses in the middle address the Prophet ﷺ about how revelation was reaching him, and the last third stops arguing to show a scene: the minutes in which someone dies.
name_story: The name comes from the first verse, where Allah swears by the Day of Resurrection. Qiyamah means the standing up, the getting to one's feet, and the surah keeps that plain sense rather than treating it as a technical term. The word appears twice in the first six verses, once as what is sworn by and once as what the denier wants a date for.

movements.note: Allah swears by the Day of Resurrection and by the self-reproaching soul, then states the objection in the deniers' own words. The answer is a detail, not an argument: the fingertips can be shaped again.
Sight is dazzled, the moon goes dark, sun and moon are joined, and the asking shifts from when to where. A person is told what he sent ahead and held back.
The address turns to the Prophet ﷺ, who had been repeating the words as they came for fear of losing them. Gathering, reciting and explaining are taken over by the One revealing.

Denial is traced to appetite, not reasoning: love of the immediate, neglect of what follows. Faces are then set beside faces, some bright and turned toward their Lord, others expecting a back-breaking blow.

Dying is shown from outside the body, with the question of who can heal him and the certainty that this is the parting. Four verses give the record: he did not affirm, he did not pray, he turned away.
The argument returns to the body. He was fluid, then a clinging form, then shaped, then made into a pair. The last verse asks whether the One who did that cannot raise the dead.

themes.t: An objection answered in its own currency
themes.d: The deniers asked about matter, so matter answers them. Bones, fingertips and the shaping of a body carry the case, and nothing is asked that cannot be checked.
Al-nafs al-lawwamah, the self that reproaches its own conduct, is named nowhere else in the Qur'an. Sworn by beside the Day of Resurrection, private reckoning sits beside public.
Verses twenty and twenty-one put denial in what is loved rather than what is known, and treat the intellectual objection as a consequence of that preference.
Five verses go to the last minutes of a life, which everyone has watched and nobody argues about. What is certain is used to make what is contested credible.

heart: The verses are very short, many of three or four words, so unhurried recitation turns the surah into statements set down one at a time with a pause after each. Anyone learning it notices where the sound changes: tight closed endings for thirty verses, then at verse thirty-one an opening into a long vowel that holds to the end.

Those four verses about the tongue shift the register completely. They were said to one person afraid of losing what he was hearing, and what he was told is that holding on to it was not his work. Readers who have struggled to keep the Qur'an in memory tend to stop there.

passages.why: The only place in the Qur'an where the self-reproaching soul is named. It gives a term to the ordinary experience of being dissatisfied with one's own conduct.
The fingertips. Resurrection is defended not by insisting bones can be gathered but by naming the smallest and most individual part of a hand.
The instruction to stop hurrying, and the undertaking that gathering, reciting and explaining belong to the One revealing. Ibn Abbas described the occasion; Sahih al-Bukhari 5.
Faces bright, turned toward their Lord and looking. Two short verses, nothing added, and the verse most cited in classical discussion of whether believers see their Lord.

connections.why: Al-Waqi'ah shows the same moment from the other side of the room, the soul at the throat while the family watch and cannot bring it back.
Ta-Ha carries the same instruction about not hastening with the Qur'an before its revelation is finished, and adds the prayer to be increased in knowledge.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a specific merit for reciting Al-Qiyamah. What is soundly recorded concerns four of its verses rather than a reward: Ibn Abbas said the Prophet ﷺ used to move his lips trying to hold what was being recited to him, and that verses sixteen to nineteen came in answer. That report is in Sahih al-Bukhari 5 and also in Sahih Muslim. This surah's standing rests on its subject, not on a promised reward.
virtue.src: no prophetic virtue report; Ibn Abbas on 75:16-19 in Bukhari 5
